claims.quote: Gonggong (/ˈɡɒŋɡɒŋ/) is a Chinese water god who is depicted in Chinese mythology and folktales as having a copper human head with an iron forehead, red hair, and the body of a serpent, or sometimes the head and torso are human, with the tail of a serpent. He is destructive and is blamed for various cosmic catastrophes.

claims.statement: His portrayal includes red hair and an iron forehead.
claims.statement_id: Penggambarannya mencakup rambut merah dan dahi besi.
claims.quote: Gonggong (/ˈɡɒŋɡɒŋ/) is a Chinese water god who is depicted in Chinese mythology and folktales as having a copper human head with an iron forehead, red hair, and the body of a serpent, or sometimes the head and torso are human, with the tail of a serpent. He is destructive and is blamed for various cosmic catastrophes.

claims.statement: The Tianwen poem blames him for altering the tilt of sky and earth; Gonggong is known from the late Warring States period (before 221 BC).
claims.statement_id: Puisi Tianwen menyalahkannya atas perubahan kemiringan langit dan bumi; Gonggong sudah dikenal sejak akhir periode Negara-Negara Berperang (sebelum 221 SM).
claims.quote: Gonggong is known from the late Warring States period (before 221 BC). Gonggong appears in the ancient "Heavenly Questions" (Tianwen) poem of the Chu Ci, where he is blamed for knocking the Earth's axis off center, causing it to tilt to the southeast and the sky to tilt to the northwest.

claims.statement: Gonggong is linked to great floods alongside his subordinate Xiangliu.
claims.statement_id: Gonggong dikaitkan dengan banjir besar bersama bawahannya Xiangliu.
claims.quote: Gonggong was credited in various mythological contexts as being responsible for great floods, often in concert with his minister Xiangliu (a.k.a. Xiangyao), who has nine heads and the body of a snake.

claims.statement: In one myth, he damages Mount Buzhou following defeat by Zhurong.
claims.statement_id: Dalam sebuah mitos, ia merusak Gunung Buzhou setelah kalah melawan Zhurong.
claims.quote: Gonggong was ashamed that he lost the fight with Zhurong, the Chinese god of fire, to claim the throne of Heaven. In a fit of rage, he smashed his head against Buzhou Mountain, one of eight pillars holding up the sky, greatly damaging it and causing the sky to tilt towards the northwest and the Earth to shift to the southeast, which caused great floods and suffering.

claims.statement: In the Classic of Mountains and Seas, Gonggong is noted as the son of Zhurong, father of Houtu and a descendant of the Flame Emperor; in a separate verse he is said to descend from the Black Emperor.
claims.statement_id: Dalam Shan Hai Jing, Gonggong disebut putra Zhurong, ayah Houtu, dan keturunan Kaisar Api; di ayat lain ia disebut keturunan Kaisar Hitam.
claims.quote: Literature from the Han dynasty becomes much more detailed regarding Gonggong. For example, within the Classic of Mountains and Seas, he is noted as being the son of Zhurong, father of Houtu, and a descendant of the Flame Emperor. However, in a separate verse, he is also said to be a descendant of the Black Emperor.

claims.statement: The goddess Nüwa cut off the legs of the giant turtle Ao and used them in place of the fallen pillar, ending the floods, but she could not fully correct the tilt of sky and earth.
claims.statement_id: Dewi Nüwa memotong kaki kura-kura raksasa Ao dan memakainya sebagai pengganti tiang yang runtuh sehingga banjir berakhir, tetapi ia tidak sepenuhnya memperbaiki kemiringan langit dan bumi.
claims.quote: The goddess Nüwa cut off the legs of the giant turtle Ao and used them in place of the fallen pillar, ending the floods and suffering; she was, however, unable to fully correct the tilted sky and Earth and alter their effects on the Sun, Moon, stars, and rivers in China.

claims.statement: Werner cites an account that toward the end of Nüwa's reign, among the feudatory princes was Kung Kung (Gonggong), who administered punishment; violent and ambitious, he rebelled and sought to overcome wood by the influence of water.
claims.statement_id: Werner mengutip catatan bahwa menjelang akhir pemerintahan Nüwa, di antara para pangeran bawahan ada Kung Kung (Gonggong) yang bertugas menjatuhkan hukuman; ia ambisius, memberontak, dan berusaha mengalahkan unsur kayu dengan pengaruh air.
claims.quote: Toward the end of her reign there was among the feudatory princes Kung Kung, whose functions were the administration of punishment. Violent and ambitious, he became a rebel, and sought by the influence of water to overcome that of wood

claims.statement: In the account Werner cites, Kung Kung fought Chu Jung (Zhurong) but did not win, then struck his head against Mount Pu Chou (Buzhou) and brought it down; the pillars of Heaven were broken and the corners of the earth gave way.
claims.statement_id: Dalam catatan yang dikutip Werner, Kung Kung berperang melawan Chu Jung (Zhurong) tetapi kalah, lalu membenturkan kepalanya ke Gunung Pu Chou (Buzhou) hingga runtuh; tiang langit patah dan sudut bumi runtuh.
claims.quote: He did battle with Chu Jung [said to have been one of the ministers of Huang Ti, and later the God of Fire], but was not victorious; whereupon he struck his head against the Imperfect Mountain, Pu Chou Shan, and brought it down. The pillars of Heaven were broken and the corners of the earth gave way.

claims.statement: Thereupon Nue Kua (Nüwa) melted stones of five colours to repair the heavens and cut off the feet of the tortoise to set upright the four extremities of the earth.
claims.statement_id: Setelah itu Nue Kua (Nüwa) melebur batu lima warna untuk memperbaiki langit dan memotong kaki kura-kura untuk menegakkan empat ujung bumi.
claims.quote: Hereupon Nue Kua melted stones of the five colours to repair the heavens, and cut off the feet of the tortoise to set upright the four extremities of the earth.

claims.statement: In Giles's translation of the Liezi, Kung Kung (Gonggong) fought Chuan Hsii (Zhuanxu) for the throne and, in his rage, blundered against Mount Pu-chou (Buzhou), snapping the pillar that connects Heaven and earth.
claims.statement_id: Dalam terjemahan Liezi oleh Giles, Kung Kung (Gonggong) berebut takhta dengan Chuan Hsii (Zhuanxu) dan, dalam amarahnya, menabrak Gunung Pu-chou (Buzhou) sehingga tiang penghubung langit dan bumi patah.
claims.quote: Later on, Kung Kung fought with Chuan Hsii for the throne, and, blundering in his rage against Mount Pu-chou, he snapped the pillar which connects Heaven and earth.

claims.statement: The Huainanzi (Tianwen Xun) says that Gonggong (共工) once contended with Zhuanxu (顓頊) to be ruler; in his rage he struck Mount Buzhou (不周之山), so that the pillar of heaven snapped and the bonds of the earth broke, whence the sky tilts to the northwest and the earth is not full in the southeast.
claims.statement_id: Huainanzi (Tianwen Xun) menyebut bahwa dahulu Gonggong (共工) berebut kedudukan penguasa dengan Zhuanxu (顓頊); dalam kemarahannya ia menabrak Gunung Buzhou (不周之山) sehingga tiang langit patah dan pengikat bumi putus, maka langit miring ke barat laut dan bumi tidak penuh di tenggara.
claims.quote: 昔者共工與顓頊爭為帝，怒而觸不周之山，天柱折，地維絕。天傾西北，故日月星辰移焉；地不滿東南，故水潦塵埃歸焉。

claims.statement: Pixiu are Chinese mythological composite creatures resembling winged lions.
claims.statement_id: Pixiu adalah makhluk campuran mitologis Tiongkok yang menyerupai singa bersayap.
claims.quote: The pixiu ([pʰǐ.ɕjóʊ]; Chinese: 貔貅) is a Chinese mythical hybrid creature. Pixiu are considered powerful protectors of the souls of the dead, xian, and feng shui practitioners, and resemble strong, winged lions.

claims.statement: Pixiu are regarded as protectors bringing good fortune and wealth.
claims.statement_id: Pixiu dianggap pelindung yang membawa keberuntungan dan kekayaan.
claims.quote: The pixiu ([pʰǐ.ɕjóʊ]; Chinese: 貔貅) is a Chinese mythical hybrid creature. Pixiu are considered powerful protectors of the souls of the dead, xian, and feng shui practitioners, and resemble strong, winged lions.

claims.statement: One division distinguishes two-antlered Bixie from single-antlered Tianlu.
claims.statement_id: Salah satu pembagian membedakan Bixie bertanduk dua dan Tianlu bertanduk satu.
claims.quote: There are two types of Pixiu that are categorised by their antlers. The one with two antlers is the female and is called a Bìxié, and the one with one antler is the male and is called a Tiānlù.

claims.statement: Their statues are used in feng shui to attract wealth.
claims.statement_id: Patungnya digunakan dalam feng shui untuk menarik kekayaan.
claims.quote: Pixiu crave the smell of gold and silver and like to bring their masters money in their mouth. Statues of this creature are often used to attract wealth in feng shui.

claims.statement: Xu Ke describes pixiu as tiger- or bear-like creatures with ashen-white fur.
claims.statement_id: Xu Ke menggambarkan pixiu menyerupai harimau atau beruang dengan bulu putih kelabu.
claims.quote: Xu Ke (徐珂) describes the 貔貅; pixiu as resembling either tigers or bears and having ashen white furs, the 貔; pi being male and the 貅; xiu female.

claims.statement: Their portrayal combines a Chinese dragon's head with a lion's body.
claims.statement_id: Penggambarannya menggabungkan kepala naga Tiongkok dengan tubuh singa.
claims.quote: They have the head of a Chinese dragon, the body of a lion, and historically sport on their heads either one antler (male) or two antlers (female).

claims.statement: An entry in this compilation describes the pi (貔) as a fierce beast of the leopard kind from the state of He (貉國), also called Zhiyi (執夷) and white fox (白狐); Guo Pu is quoted as saying a classic compares fierce beasts to tigers and the pi.
claims.statement_id: Sebuah entri dalam kompilasi ini menyebut pi (貔) sebagai binatang buas golongan macan tutul dari negeri He (貉國), yang juga disebut Zhiyi (執夷) dan rubah putih (白狐); Guo Pu dikutip menyebut kitab klasik membandingkan binatang buas dengan harimau dan pi.
claims.quote: 貔，豹屬，猛獸，出貉國，一名執夷，一名白狐。郭璞云：「《書》 稱猛獸如虎如貔。」貔蓋豹屬，亦曰執夷。

claims.statement: The same entry quotes the Shiji (Wudi Benji): the Yellow Emperor of the You Xiong clan trained bears, brown bears, pixiu (貔貅), chu (貙) and tigers to fight the Yan Emperor in the wilds of Banquan.
claims.statement_id: Entri yang sama mengutip Shiji (Wudi Benji): Huangdi dari klan You Xiong melatih beruang, beruang cokelat, pixiu (貔貅), chu (貙), dan harimau untuk berperang melawan Kaisar Yan di padang Banquan.
claims.quote: 《史記·五帝本紀》：「黃帝有熊氏，教熊羆貔貅貙虎，以與 炎帝戰於阪泉之野。」

claims.statement: The entry also quotes the Liji (Quli): "if there are fierce beasts ahead, carry the pixiu"; the commentary says fierce beasts are of the tiger and wolf kind, the pixiu are also fierce, and this is raised so that people know to be prepared.
claims.statement_id: Entri itu juga mengutip Liji (Quli): "bila di depan ada binatang buas, bawalah pixiu"; catatan tafsir menyebut binatang buas tergolong harimau dan serigala, pixiu juga garang, dan hal ini ditunjukkan agar orang tahu bersiap.
claims.quote: 《禮記·曲禮》：「前有摯獸，則載貔貅。」〈注〉摯獸虎狼之屬，貔 貅亦有威猛，舉此使眾知為備

claims.statement: In the quotation from the Maoshi Lushu Guangyao, the pi is said to resemble a tiger or, as some say, a bear; it is also called Zhiyi and white fox, and the people of Liaodong call its young "white bear" (白羆).
claims.statement_id: Dalam kutipan dari Maoshi Lushu Guangyao, pi digambarkan menyerupai harimau atau, menurut sebagian orang, beruang; juga disebut Zhiyi dan rubah putih, dan orang Liaodong menyebut anaknya "beruang putih" (白羆).
claims.quote: 貔似虎，或曰似熊，一名「執夷」，一名「白狐。」其子為 遼 東人謂之「白羆。」

claims.statement: Baku are Japanese supernatural creatures believed to consume nightmares.
claims.statement_id: Baku adalah makhluk gaib Jepang yang dipercaya memakan mimpi buruk.
claims.quote: Baku (獏 or 貘) are Japanese supernatural beings that are said to devour nightmares. They originate from the Chinese Mo. According to legend, they were created by the spare pieces that were left over when the gods finished creating all other animals. They have a long history in Japanese folklore and art, and more recently have appeared in manga and anime.

claims.statement: Baku's origin is linked to Chinese mo and a tale about leftover pieces from animal creation.
claims.statement_id: Asal baku dihubungkan dengan mo Tiongkok dan kisah sisa bahan penciptaan hewan.
claims.quote: Baku (獏 or 貘) are Japanese supernatural beings that are said to devour nightmares. They originate from the Chinese Mo. According to legend, they were created by the spare pieces that were left over when the gods finished creating all other animals. They have a long history in Japanese folklore and art, and more recently have appeared in manga and anime.

claims.statement: The term baku denotes both the dream-eating creature and the Malayan tapir.
claims.statement_id: Istilah baku juga dipakai untuk tapir Malaya, selain makhluk pemakan mimpi.
claims.quote: The Japanese term baku has two current meanings, referring to both the traditional dream-devouring creature and to the Malayan tapir.  In recent years, there have been changes in how the baku is depicted.

claims.statement: Baku were known in Japan by the Muromachi period.
claims.statement_id: Baku sudah dikenal di Jepang pada zaman Muromachi.
claims.quote: The traditional Japanese nightmare-devouring baku originates in Chinese folklore from the mo 貘 and was familiar in Japan as early as the Muromachi period (14th–15th century). Hori Tadao has described the dream-eating abilities attributed to the traditional baku and relates them to other preventatives against nightmare such as amulets.

claims.statement: The Sankai Ibutsu manuscript describes an elephant's trunk and tusks with rhinoceros ears.
claims.statement_id: Naskah Sankai Ibutsu menggambarkan belalai serta gading gajah dan telinga badak.
claims.quote: describes the baku as a shy, Chinese mythical chimera with the trunk and tusks of an elephant, the ears of a rhinoceros, the tail of a cow, the body of a bear and the paws of a tiger, which protected against pestilence and evil, although eating nightmares was not included among its abilities.

claims.statement: Lafcadio Hearn wrote about a nightmare-eating baku in 1902.
claims.statement_id: Lafcadio Hearn menulis tentang baku pemakan mimpi buruk pada 1902.
claims.quote:
Writing in the Meiji period, Lafcadio Hearn (1902) described a baku with very similar attributes that was also able to devour nightmares.
Legend has it that a person who wakes up from a bad dream can call out to baku.

claims.statement: Hearn writes that the creature is named Baku, or Shirokinakatsukami, and that its particular function is eating dreams.
claims.statement_id: Hearn menulis bahwa makhluk ini bernama Baku atau Shirokinakatsukami, dan fungsinya yang khas adalah memakan mimpi.
claims.quote: The name of the creature is Baku, or Shirokinakatsukami; and its particular function is the eating of Dreams.

claims.statement: According to an ancient book in Hearn's possession, the male baku has a horse's body, a lion's face, an elephant's trunk and tusks, a rhinoceros's forelock, a cow's tail and a tiger's feet.
claims.statement_id: Menurut sebuah buku kuno milik Hearn, baku jantan bertubuh kuda, berwajah singa, berbelalai dan bergading seperti gajah, berjambul badak, berekor sapi, dan berkaki harimau.
claims.quote: An ancient book in my possession states that the male Baku has the body of a horse, the face of a lion, the trunk and tusks of an elephant, the forelock of a rhinoceros, the tail of a cow, and the feet of a tiger.

claims.statement: According to Hearn, the Chinese character for the name baku used to be written in gold on the lacquered wooden pillows of lords and princes, and the sleeper was thought to be protected from evil dreams.
claims.statement_id: Menurut Hearn, aksara Tiongkok untuk nama baku dahulu dituliskan dengan emas pada bantal kayu berlak milik para bangsawan dan pangeran, dan pemakainya dianggap terlindung dari mimpi buruk.
claims.quote: the Chinese character representing its name used to be put in gold upon the lacquered wooden pillows of lords and princes. By the virtue and power of this character on the pillow, the sleeper was thought to be protected from evil dreams.

claims.statement: Hearn records an old invocation to the baku still in common use: "Baku kuraë!", meaning "Devour, O Baku! devour my evil dream!"
claims.statement_id: Hearn mencatat seruan lama kepada baku yang masih dipakai sehari-hari: "Baku kuraë!", yang berarti "Lahaplah, wahai Baku, mimpi burukku!"
claims.quote: the old invocation to the Baku still survives in common parlance: Baku kuraë! Baku kuraë!--"Devour, O Baku! devour my evil dream!"

claims.statement: According to Hearn, a person waking from a nightmare should quickly repeat the invocation three times, after which the baku will eat the dream and change the misfortune or fear into good fortune and gladness.
claims.statement_id: Menurut Hearn, orang yang terbangun dari mimpi buruk hendaknya cepat mengulang seruan itu tiga kali, lalu baku akan memakan mimpi itu dan mengubah kemalangan atau ketakutan menjadi keberuntungan dan kegembiraan.
claims.quote: When you awake from a nightmare, or from any unlucky dream, you should quickly repeat that invocation three times;--then the Baku will eat the dream, and will change the misfortune or the fear into good fortune and gladness.

claims.statement: In the time of the old Chinese learning, pictures of the baku used to be hung in Japanese houses, being supposed to exert the same beneficent power as the creature itself.
claims.statement_id: Pada masa pengaruh pembelajaran Tiongkok kuno, gambar baku dahulu digantung di rumah-rumah Jepang karena dianggap memiliki daya baik yang sama dengan makhluknya sendiri.
claims.quote: In the time of the old Chinese learning, pictures of the Baku used to be hung up in Japanese houses, such pictures being supposed to exert the same beneficent power as the creature itself.

claims.statement: Gumiho belongs to East Asian folktales and Korean legends, resembling Chinese jiuweihu and Japanese kitsune.
claims.statement_id: Gumiho adalah makhluk dalam cerita Asia Timur dan legenda Korea, sejenis dengan jiuweihu Tiongkok dan kitsune Jepang.
claims.quote: is a creature that appears in the folktales of East Asia and legends of Korea. It is similar to the Chinese jiuweihu, the Japanese kitsune and the Vietnamese hồ ly tinh.

claims.statement: The designation was used for magical foxes in Joseon-era novels.
claims.statement_id: Sebutan ini digunakan untuk rubah ajaib dalam novel zaman Joseon.
claims.quote: Gumiho is a term that originally referred to a magical fox appearing in Korean novels of the Joseon dynasty, or was used pejoratively in historical records of the same period to denounce treacherous officials. In modern Korea, the designation gumiho has been broadened to encompass all fox spirits described in traditional Korean sources.

claims.statement: In colloquial Korean, gumiho may describe someone regarded as cunning.
claims.statement_id: Dalam percakapan Korea, gumiho juga dapat menyebut orang yang dianggap licik.
claims.quote: In Korean colloquial usage, gumiho is often applied to describe a person (especially a woman) regarded as sly or cunning.

claims.statement: Korean tradition includes fox spirits beyond the nine-tailed type.
claims.statement_id: Tidak semua roh rubah dalam tradisi Korea memiliki sembilan ekor.
claims.quote: hite fox"), maegu (매구, "fox demon"), and hogwi (호귀, "fox ghost"), all of which, like gumiho, have also been employed in a derogatory sense when referring to women. As these various names indicate, the types of foxes appearing in Korean mythology are diverse and are not limited to the nine-tailed fox (gumiho).

claims.statement: Tales usually portray foxes as deceptive or tragic, though benevolent variants exist.
claims.statement_id: Kisah biasanya menggambarkan rubah sebagai penipu atau makhluk tragis, meski ada varian baik.
claims.quote: In Korean myth, foxes are primarily depicted as deceptive, malevolent, and tragic beings, though there are rare cases where they are portrayed as benevolent toward humans or as deities governing mountains.

claims.statement: Fox spirits often appear as beautiful women or heretical monks.
claims.statement_id: Roh rubah sering mengambil rupa perempuan cantik atau biksu sesat.
claims.quote: They are often portrayed in the form of heretical Buddhist monks or beautiful women and are sometimes depicted as monsters that torment and threaten dragons, which are considered sacred in Korean mythology.

claims.statement: According to the Encyclopedia of Korean Culture, the fox-orb tale belongs to the transformation tales, is distributed nationwide, and is also known as "The limits of human knowledge" or "The gumiho (구미호) and the yeouiju (wish-granting jewel)".
claims.statement_id: Menurut Ensiklopedia Kebudayaan Korea, kisah Yeou-guseul (kisah manik rubah) termasuk kisah perubahan wujud, tersebar di seluruh negeri, dan juga dikenal dengan judul "Batas pengetahuan manusia" atau "Gumiho (구미호) dan yeouiju (manik pengabul)".
claims.quote: 신이담(神異譚) 중 변신담에 속한다. 전국적인 분포를 보이며 ‘인지(人智)의 한계’ 또는 ‘구미호와 여의주’·‘여우 입 속의 보배 구슬’이라고도 한다.

claims.statement: According to the encyclopedia, tales about the gumiho are reported to be especially widely transmitted in the Hamgyeong, Pyeongan, and Hwanghae regions.
claims.statement_id: Menurut ensiklopedia itu, kisah tentang gumiho dilaporkan terutama banyak diwariskan di wilayah Hamgyeong, Pyeongan, dan Hwanghae.
claims.quote: ‘구미호’에 관한 설화는 함경도·평안도·황해도 지역에 특히 많이 전승되는 것으로 보고되어 있다.

claims.statement: In the first type of the tale, a village-school student meets and falls in love with a pretty girl; because she will not allow a kiss he realizes she is a gumiho, threatens never to see her again, and after she reluctantly consents he takes the yeouiju from her mouth.
claims.statement_id: Dalam tipe pertama kisah itu, seorang murid sekolah desa bertemu gadis cantik dan jatuh cinta; karena ia tidak mau dicium, sang murid menyadari bahwa ia gumiho, mengancam tidak akan menemuinya lagi, dan setelah gadis itu terpaksa mengizinkan, sang murid mengambil yeouiju dari mulutnya.
claims.quote: 한 학동이 서당을 다니다가 예쁜 처녀를 만나 사랑하게 되었다. 처녀가 입맞춤만은 허락하지 않으므로 구미호라는 것을 알게 된다. 학동은 입맞춤을 허락하지 않으면 다시는 만나지 않겠다고 위협하였다. 어쩔 수 없이 처녀가 허락하자, 학동은 처녀의 입 속에서 여의주를 꺼내 물었다.

claims.statement: In the second type of the tale, a fox that could ascend to heaven by killing 100 students with kisses transforms into a woman and visits the village school at midnight.
claims.statement_id: Dalam tipe kedua kisah itu, seekor rubah yang konon dapat naik ke langit bila membunuh 100 murid dengan ciuman berubah menjadi perempuan dan mendatangi sekolah desa pada tengah malam.
claims.quote: 학동 100명을 입맞춤하여 죽이면 승천할 수 있다는 여우가 여자로 변신하여 한밤중에 서당을 찾아갔다.

claims.statement: According to the encyclopedia, many folk traditions about foxes have been handed down, mainly about the gumiho (九尾狐) and the like, which appear as uncanny beings that use sorcery to torment humans.
claims.statement_id: Menurut ensiklopedia itu, banyak tradisi rakyat tentang rubah diwariskan, terutama tentang gumiho (九尾狐) dan sejenisnya, yang tampil sebagai makhluk gaib yang memakai sihir untuk mengganggu manusia.
claims.quote: 여우에 대한 많은 민간전승이 내려오고 있는데, 주로 구미호(九尾狐) ... 등 조화를 부려 인간을 괴롭히는 요물로 나타난다.

claims.statement: Huli jing are shapeshifting fox spirits of Chinese mythology.
claims.statement_id: Huli jing adalah roh rubah dalam mitologi Tiongkok yang dapat berubah wujud.

claims.statement: Fox spirits may be benevolent or malevolent.

claims.statement: Dokkaebi are Korean legendary beings who interact with people through assistance or tricks.
claims.statement_id: Dokkaebi adalah makhluk legenda Korea yang berinteraksi dengan manusia melalui pertolongan atau tipu daya.
claims.quote: Dokkaebi (Korean: 도깨비) are legendary creatures from Korean mythology and folklore. Dokkaebi, also known as "Korean ogres", are nature deities or spirits possessing extraordinary powers and abilities that are used to interact with humans, at times playing tricks on them and at times helping them.

claims.statement: The tale of Lady Dohwa and Bachelor Bihyeong provides early documentation of dokkaebi.
claims.statement_id: Kisah Lady Dohwa dan Bachelor Bihyeong menjadi dokumentasi awal dokkaebi.
claims.quote: The earliest known documentation of dokkaebi is in the Silla-era tale of "Lady Dohwa and Bachelor Bihyeong" from the Memorabilia of the Three Kingdoms compiled during the Goryeo period. Dokkaebi are featured in many folk tale anthologies compiled during the Joseon period.

claims.statement: Dokkaebi differ from human ghosts; some arise through possession of inanimate objects.
claims.statement_id: Dokkaebi dibedakan dari hantu manusia; sebagian muncul melalui benda mati yang dirasuki.
claims.quote: Dokkaebi are different from deities, divinities, spirits or ghosts, called gwishin (귀신) in Korean, in that they are not formed by the death of a human being, but rather by the spiritual possession of an inanimate object such as old discarded household tools like brooms, or objects stained with human blood.

claims.statement: Some tales describe ssireum wrestling challenges to travelers.
claims.statement_id: Beberapa kisah menggambarkan tantangan gulat ssireum kepada pengelana.
claims.quote: Different versions of the dokkaebi mythology assign different attributes to them. In some cases, they are considered harmless but nevertheless mischievous, usually playing pranks on people or challenging wayward travelers to a ssireum (Korean wrestling) match for the right to pass. Dokkaebi are extremely skilled at wrestling and cannot be beaten unless their right side is exploited.

claims.statement: Glimmering light or blue flames may herald a dokkaebi's appearance.
claims.statement_id: Cahaya atau nyala biru dapat menandai kedatangan dokkaebi.
claims.quote: Dokkaebi fire is a glimmering light or tall blue flames that herald the appearance of dokkaebi.

claims.statement: Their magical objects include an invisibility hat and a club that summons things.
claims.statement_id: Benda ajaibnya mencakup topi pemberi ketakterlihatan dan tongkat pemuncul barang.
claims.quote: Dokkaebi possess magical items, such as the dokkaebi hat called the dokkaebi gamtu (도깨비 감투), which grants the wearer the ability of invisibility, and the dokkaebi magic club called the dokkaebi bangmangi (도깨비 방망이), which can summon things and act functionally as a magic wand. Dokkaebi like buckwheat jelly, sorghum and red bean rice cakes, mashed sorghum, and the drinks.

claims.statement: Korea.net describes dokkaebi as playful and says some bring treasure using their clubs.
claims.statement_id: Korea.net menyebut dokkaebi cenderung bermain-main dan sebagian membawa harta melalui tongkatnya.
claims.quote: Goblins are called dokkaebi in Korea. Unlike other monsters, these dokkaebi are more playful than harmful, and some of them bring you treasure with their club.

claims.statement: Taotie is a Chinese mythological creature counted among the Four Perils.
claims.statement_id: Taotie adalah makhluk mitologis Tiongkok yang termasuk Empat Bahaya.
claims.quote: The taotie is an ancient Chinese mythological creature that was commonly emblazoned on bronze and other artifacts during the 1st millennium BCE. Taotie are one of the Four Perils in Chinese classics like the Classic of Mountains and Seas, alongside the Hundun, Qiongqi, and Taowu.

claims.statement: Bronze-vessel motifs depict a symmetrical animal mask with raised eyes.
claims.statement_id: Motif pada bejana perunggu menampilkan topeng hewan simetris dengan mata menonjol.
claims.quote: The Taotie is often represented as a motif on dings, which are Chinese ritual bronze vessels from the Shang (c. 1600 – c. 1050 BCE) and Zhou dynasties (c. 1046 – 256 BCE). The design typically consists of a zoomorphic mask, described as being frontal, bilaterally symmetrical, with a pair of raised eyes and typically no lower jaw area.

claims.statement: The name used by Shang and Zhou people for the motif is unknown.
claims.statement_id: Nama yang dipakai masyarakat Shang dan Zhou untuk motif tersebut tidak diketahui.
claims.quote: Although modern scholars use the word taotie, it is actually not known what word the Shang and Zhou dynasties used to call the design on their bronze vessels; as American paleographer Sarah Allan notes, there is no particular reason to assume that the term taotie was known during the Shang period.

claims.statement: The Zuo Zhuan associates taotie with gluttony.
claims.statement_id: Zuo Zhuan mengaitkan taotie dengan kerakusan.
claims.quote: Within the Zuo Zhuan, taotie is used by the writer to imply gluttony.

claims.statement: A quoted Lüshi Chunqiu passage describes a head without a body on Zhou bronzes.
claims.statement_id: Kutipan Lüshi Chunqiu menggambarkan kepala tanpa tubuh pada perunggu Zhou.
claims.quote: The taotie on Zhou bronzes [ding] has a head but no body. When it eats people, it does not swallow them, but harms them.

claims.statement: Li Zehou interprets taotie imagery as mysterious communication between people and heaven.
claims.statement_id: Li Zehou menafsirkan motif taotie sebagai komunikasi misterius antara manusia dan langit.
claims.quote: Li Zehou, a Chinese scholar of philosophy and intellectual history, thinks the description of the taotie in the Lüshi Chunqiu has a much deeper meaning, and that "the meaning of taotie is not [about] 'eating people' but making a mysterious communication between people and Heaven (gods)."

claims.statement: The Zuo Zhuan (春秋左氏傳) tells of an untalented son (不才子) of the Jinyun clan (縉雲氏) who was greedy for food and drink (貪于飲食) and covetous of goods (冒于貨賄); the people of the world compared him with the three ills (三凶) and called him 饕餮 (taotie).
claims.statement_id: Zuo Zhuan (春秋左氏傳) menyebut seorang anak tak berbakat (不才子) dari keluarga Jinyun (縉雲氏) yang rakus makanan dan minuman (貪于飲食) serta tamak harta (冒于貨賄); orang-orang di dunia membandingkannya dengan tiga keburukan (三凶) dan menyebutnya 饕餮.
claims.quote: 縉雲氏有不才子，貪于飲食，冒于貨賄，侵欲崇侈，不可盈厭，聚斂積實，不知紀極，不分孤寡，不恤窮匱，天下之民，以比三凶，謂之饕餮

claims.statement: The Zuo Zhuan says that Shun (舜), as minister to Yao (堯), banished the four evil clans (四凶族): Hundun (渾敦), Qiongqi (窮奇), Taowu (檮杌) and Taotie (饕餮), casting them to the four frontiers (四裔) to ward off 螭魅.
claims.statement_id: Zuo Zhuan menyebut bahwa Shun (舜), sebagai menteri Yao (堯), mengusir empat kaum jahat (四凶族): Hundun (渾敦), Qiongqi (窮奇), Taowu (檮杌), dan Taotie (饕餮), melemparkan mereka ke empat penjuru tepi (四裔) untuk menangkal 螭魅.
claims.quote: 舜臣堯，賓于四門，流四凶族，渾敦，窮奇，檮杌，饕餮，投諸四裔，以禦螭魅

claims.statement: The Lüshi Chunqiu (呂氏春秋) says that the Zhou tripod (周鼎) bears (著) a taotie (饕餮) with a head but no body (有首無身); before it has swallowed the people it eats (食人未咽) harm has reached its own body (害及其身). The next sentence says that doing wrong is likewise (為不善亦然).
claims.statement_id: Lüshi Chunqiu (呂氏春秋) menyebut bahwa pada tripod Zhou (周鼎) terukir (著) taotie (饕餮) yang berkepala tetapi tak bertubuh (有首無身); ia belum menelan manusia yang dimakannya (食人未咽) tetapi sudah mencelakai tubuhnya sendiri (害及其身). Kalimat berikutnya: berbuat tidak baik pun demikian (為不善亦然).
claims.quote: 周鼎著饕餮，有首無身，食人未咽，害及其身，以言報更也。為不善亦然。

claims.statement: The three-legged crow is an East Asian mythological creature representing the sun.
claims.statement_id: Gagak berkaki tiga adalah makhluk mitologis Asia Timur yang mewakili matahari.
claims.quote: The three-legged (or tripedal) crow is a mythological creature in various mythologies and arts of East Asia. It is believed to inhabit and represent the Sun.

claims.statement: Chinese tales use Yangwu and Jinwu for the sun crow.
claims.statement_id: Dalam kisah Tiongkok, nama Yangwu dan Jinwu merujuk pada gagak matahari.
claims.quote: The Chinese have several versions of crow and crow-Sun tales. But the most popular depiction and myth of the Sun crow is that of the Yangwu or Jinwu, the "golden crow". It has also been found figured on ancient coins from Lycia and Pamphylia.

claims.statement: The Shanhaijing includes a reference to the three-legged crow.
claims.statement_id: Shanhaijing memuat penyebutan gagak berkaki tiga.
claims.quote: It is also mentioned in the Shanhaijing. The earliest known depiction of a three-legged crow appears in Neolithic pottery of the Yangshao culture.

claims.statement: The crow in a solar disc appears among symbols on formal imperial garments.
claims.statement_id: Gagak dalam cakram matahari muncul pada lambang pakaian resmi kekaisaran.
claims.quote: The sanzuwu in a disc represents the sun and is also one of the Twelve Ornaments that is used in the decoration of formal imperial garments in ancient China.

claims.statement: The sun crow is often colored red despite the name golden crow.
claims.statement_id: Gagak matahari sering diberi warna merah meski disebut gagak emas.
claims.quote: The most popular depiction and myth of a sanzuwu is of a sun crow called the Yangwu (陽烏), more commonly referred to as the Jinwu (金烏; 'golden crow') or "golden crow". Even though it is described as a corvid, it is usually coloured red instead of black.

claims.statement: This crow is also portrayed with the Queen Mother of the West.
claims.statement_id: Gagak ini juga digambarkan bersama Ibu Suri dari Barat.
claims.quote: The sanzuwu is also depicted with the Queen Mother of the West who are believed to be her messengers.

claims.statement: The Taiping Yulan (太平御覽) quotes the Lunheng (論衡): the scholars (儒者) say there is a three-legged crow (三足烏) in the sun; the sun is fire and a crow entering fire would be scorched, yet the crow is the "qi of the sun" (日氣).
claims.statement_id: Taiping Yulan (太平御覽) mengutip Lunheng (論衡): kaum sarjana (儒者) mengatakan di dalam matahari ada burung gagak berkaki tiga (三足烏); matahari adalah api, dan gagak yang masuk ke dalam api akan hangus, tetapi gagak adalah "qi matahari" (日氣).
claims.quote: 《論衡》曰：儒者言：日中有三足烏。日，火也。烏入火中燋爛，安得立？然烏，日氣也。

claims.statement: The Taiping Yulan quotes the Lingxian (靈憲) of Zhang Heng (張衡): the sun is the ancestor of the yang essence (陽精之宗), which accumulates and becomes a crow; the crow has three toes (三趾), and the number is of the odd kind belonging to yang.
claims.statement_id: Taiping Yulan mengutip Lingxian (靈憲) karya Zhang Heng (張衡): matahari adalah induk esensi "yang" (陽精之宗), yang menumpuk dan menjadi gagak; gagak punya tiga jari kaki (三趾), dan angka itu tergolong ganjil seperti bilangan "yang" (陽之數類竒).
claims.quote: 張衡《靈憲》曰：日，陽精之宗，積而成烏。烏有三趾，陽之數類竒。

claims.statement: The Taiping Yulan quotes the Kuodi tu (括地圗): in the Ruoshui waters of Kunlun, which cannot be reached without riding a dragon, there is a divine three-legged crow (三足神烏) that fetches food for Xiwangmu (西王母, Queen Mother of the West).
claims.statement_id: Taiping Yulan mengutip Kuodi tu (括地圗): di perairan Ruoshui di Kunlun, yang tak bisa dicapai tanpa menunggang naga, ada gagak gaib berkaki tiga (三足神烏) yang mengambilkan makanan bagi Xiwangmu (西王母).
claims.quote: 《括地圗》曰：崑崙之弱水中，非乘龍不得至。有三足神烏，為西王母取食。

claims.statement: The Taiping Yulan quotes the Daren fu (大人賦) of Sima Xiangru (司馬相如): the poet sees Xiwangmu (西王母), white-haired, wearing a sheng headdress (戴勝) and living in a cave, with a three-legged crow (三足烏) serving as her messenger (為之使).
claims.statement_id: Taiping Yulan mengutip Daren fu (大人賦) karya Sima Xiangru (司馬相如): sang penyair melihat Xiwangmu (西王母) beruban putih, bermahkota sheng (戴勝), tinggal di gua, dan seekor gagak berkaki tiga (三足烏) menjadi suruhannya (為之使).
claims.quote: 司馬相如《大人賦》曰：吾乃覩西王母，皜然白首母，戴勝而穴處，有三足烏為之使。

claims.statement: The Taiping Yulan quotes the Huainanzi (淮南子): in the time of Yao (堯) ten suns appeared together; Yao ordered Yi (羿) to shoot at the ten suns and he hit nine of them, whereupon the crows (烏) all died and their wings fell.
claims.statement_id: Taiping Yulan mengutip Huainanzi (淮南子): pada zaman Yao (堯) sepuluh matahari muncul bersamaan; Yao menyuruh Yi (羿) memanah sepuluh matahari itu dan mengenai sembilan di antaranya, lalu semua gagak (烏) mati dan sayapnya jatuh.
claims.quote: 《淮南子》曰：堯時，十日並出。堯命羿仰射十日，中其九。烏皆死，墮其翼。

claims.statement: The Taiping Yulan quotes the Tang shu (唐書): in the first year of Tianshou (天授) someone presented a three-legged crow, and Tianhou (天后) took it as an auspicious response for the Zhou house (周室嘉應); Ruizong (睿宗), then the imperial heir (皇嗣), said the crow's front foot was false (偽), and shortly afterwards one foot fell to the ground.
claims.statement_id: Taiping Yulan mengutip Tang shu (唐書): pada tahun pertama Tianshou (天授) seseorang mempersembahkan gagak berkaki tiga dan Tianhou (天后) menganggapnya pertanda baik bagi dinasti Zhou (周室嘉應); Ruizong (睿宗), yang kala itu putra mahkota (皇嗣), berkata kaki depan gagak itu palsu (偽), dan tak lama kemudian satu kaki jatuh ke tanah.
claims.quote: 《唐書》曰： 天授元年，有進三足烏者，天后以為周室嘉應。睿宗時為皇嗣，言曰：「烏前足偽也。」天后不恱。須臾，一足墮地，果如其言。

claims.statement: The Shanhaijing (山海經), Dahuang dong jing, says that at Tanggu (湯谷) there is a fusang tree (扶木); as one sun arrives another goes out, and all are carried by crows (載于烏).
claims.statement_id: Shanhaijing (山海經), Dahuang dong jing, menyebut di Tanggu (湯谷) ada pohon fusang (扶木); ketika satu matahari tiba, satu matahari lain keluar, dan semuanya dibawa oleh gagak (載于烏).
claims.quote: 大荒之中，有山名曰孽搖頵羝，上有扶木，柱三百里，其葉如芥。有谷曰溫源谷。湯谷上有扶木。一日方至，一日方出，皆載于烏。

claims.statement: Yeren is an unconfirmed creature described as hairy, human-like, and bipedal.
claims.statement_id: Yeren adalah makhluk tak terkonfirmasi yang digambarkan mirip manusia, berbulu, dan berjalan dengan dua kaki.
claims.quote: 野人（やじん、中国語: 野人、英語: Yeren）とは、未確認動物（UMA）の一種。雪男やビッグフットと同様に、人間に近い体格で二足歩行をし、なおかつ体表が毛に覆われているという外見的特徴を持つとされる。このため、現存する猿人（ラマピテクスなど）あるいは原人ではないかという憶測がなされている。

claims.statement: Reported sightings are especially associated with Shennongjia in Hubei, China.
claims.statement_id: Laporan penampakan terutama dikaitkan dengan Shennongjia di Hubei, Tiongkok.
claims.quote: 目撃報告は中国、特に湖北省神農架地区に多く見られている。ただし、捕獲や射殺をしたという伝聞は残っているものの、実際に生物学的な検証が行われた例は知られていない。中国科学院が神農架地区で過去に学術調査を行ったが、野人を発見することはできなかった。中国・湖北省で、野人を追う研究団体HWMRAが、世界中から新たなメンバーを募っている（2010年10月10日現在）。

claims.statement: The article reports that academic surveys failed to find Yeren and records no biological confirmation.
claims.statement_id: Artikel menyebut survei akademis belum menemukan Yeren dan tidak mencatat konfirmasi biologis.
claims.quote: 目撃報告は中国、特に湖北省神農架地区に多く見られている。ただし、捕獲や射殺をしたという伝聞は残っているものの、実際に生物学的な検証が行われた例は知られていない。中国科学院が神農架地区で過去に学術調査を行ったが、野人を発見することはできなかった。中国・湖北省で、野人を追う研究団体HWMRAが、世界中から新たなメンバーを募っている（2010年10月10日現在）。

claims.statement: Proposed explanations include mistaken identification of monkeys and fabricated reports.
claims.statement_id: Salah identifikasi kera dan cerita rekaan termasuk penjelasan yang diajukan.
claims.quote: また、目撃証言も信憑性の低いものが非常に多いとされる。現在では、既存のサルの誤認、狂言説が有力。

claims.statement: The Bencao Gangmu (本草綱目), with Li Shizhen (時珍) quoting the Fangyu zhi (《方輿志》), says the 狒狒 also exists in the mountains of Xishu and Chuzhou and is called 人熊; at Youshan in Shaxian in the Min region (閩中) one is more than a 丈 long, laughs on meeting people, is called 山大人, or is said to be a 野人 and 山魈.
claims.statement_id: Bencao Gangmu (本草綱目), dengan Li Shizhen (時珍) mengutip Fangyu zhi (《方輿志》), menyebut bahwa 狒狒 juga ada di pegunungan Xishu dan Chuzhou dan disebut 人熊; di Youshan, Shaxian, wilayah Min (閩中), ada yang panjangnya lebih dari 丈, tertawa saat bertemu orang, disebut 山大人, atau dikatakan sebagai 野人 dan 山魈.
claims.quote: 時珍曰︰按《方輿志》云︰狒狒，西蜀及處州山中亦有之，呼為人熊。人亦食其掌，剝其皮。閩中沙縣幼山有之，長丈餘，逢人則笑，呼為山大人，或曰野人及山魈也。

claims.statement: The Bencao Gangmu quotes Luo Yuan (羅願) in the Erya yi (《爾雅翼》) that present-day accounts of the xingxing (猩猩) are not far from the 狒狒: like a woman with loose hair and bare feet, without knees, walking in groups and covering its form with its hands on meeting people; this is called a 野人.
claims.statement_id: Bencao Gangmu mengutip Luo Yuan (羅願) dalam Erya yi (《爾雅翼》) bahwa uraian masa kini tentang xingxing (猩猩) tak jauh dari 狒狒: seperti perempuan berambut terurai dan berkaki telanjang, tanpa lutut, berjalan berkelompok, dan menutupi tubuhnya dengan tangan saat bertemu orang; makhluk ini disebut 野人.
claims.quote: 又羅願《爾雅翼》云︰古之說猩猩者，如豕、如狗、如猴。今之說猩猩者，與狒狒不相遠。云如婦人被髮袒足，無膝群行，遇人則手掩其形，謂之野人。

claims.statement: The Four Symbols are a group of four mythological directional guardians in Chinese constellations.
claims.statement_id: Four Symbols adalah kelompok empat makhluk mitologis penjaga arah dalam rasi Tiongkok.
claims.quote: The Four Symbols  are mythological creatures appearing among the Chinese constellations along the ecliptic, and viewed as the guardians of the four cardinal directions. These four creatures are also referred to by a variety of other names, including "Four Guardians", "Four Gods", and "Four Auspicious Beasts".

claims.statement: The group comprises Azure Dragon, Vermilion Bird, White Tiger, and Black Turtle-Snake.
claims.statement_id: Kelompok ini terdiri atas Naga Biru, Burung Merah, Harimau Putih, dan Kura-kura Hitam.
claims.quote: The members of said group consist of the Azure Dragon of the East, the Vermilion Bird of the South, the White Tiger of the West, and the Black Turtle-Snake (also called "Black Warrior") of the North.

claims.statement: Each member is linked to a direction, color, season, and element.
claims.statement_id: Masing-masing anggota dihubungkan dengan arah, warna, musim, dan unsur.
claims.quote: Each of the creatures is most closely associated with a cardinal direction and a color, but also additionally represents other aspects, including a season of the year, an emotion, virtue, and one of the Chinese "five elements" (wood, fire, metal, and water; earth is often excluded). Each has been given its own individual traits, origin story and a reason for being.

claims.statement: In Taoism, the four symbols also receive human identities and names.
claims.statement_id: Dalam Taoisme, empat lambang juga diberi identitas dan nama manusia.
claims.quote: In Taoism, the Four Symbols have been assigned human identities and names. The Azure Dragon is named Meng Zhang (孟章), the Vermilion Bird is called Ling Guang (陵光), the White Tiger Jian Bing (監兵), and the Black Turtle-Snake Zhi Ming (執明). Its Japanese equivalent, in corresponding order: Seiryū (east), Suzaku (south), Byakko (west), Genbu (north).

claims.statement: The Huainanzi (Tianwen xun) records that the east (element wood) has as its beast (獸) the Canglong (蒼龍, azure dragon) and the south (element fire) has the Zhuniao (朱鳥, vermilion bird).
claims.statement_id: Huainanzi (Tianwen xun) mencatat bahwa arah timur (unsur kayu) memiliki "hewan" (獸) Canglong (蒼龍, naga biru-hijau), dan arah selatan (unsur api) memiliki Zhuniao (朱鳥, burung merah).
claims.quote: 東方，木也，其帝太皞，其佐句芒，執規而治春。其神為歲星，其獸蒼龍，其音角，其日甲乙。南方，火也，其帝炎帝，其佐朱明，執衡而治夏。其神為熒惑，其獸朱鳥，其音徵，其日丙丁。

claims.statement: The Huainanzi (Tianwen xun) records that the west (element metal) has the Baihu (白虎, white tiger) and the north (element water) has the Xuanwu (玄武).
claims.statement_id: Huainanzi (Tianwen xun) mencatat bahwa arah barat (unsur logam) memiliki Baihu (白虎, harimau putih), dan arah utara (unsur air) memiliki Xuanwu (玄武).
claims.quote: 西方，金也，其帝少昊，其佐蓐收，執矩而治秋。其神為太白，其獸白虎，其音商，其日庚辛。北方，水也，其帝顓頊，其佐玄冥，執權而治冬。其神為辰星，其獸玄武，其音羽，其日壬癸。

claims.statement: The Liji (Quli shang) says that on the march Xuanwu (玄武) is behind, the Azure Dragon (青龍) on the left and the White Tiger (白虎) on the right, with Zhaoyao (招摇) above.
claims.statement_id: Liji (Quli shang) menyebut bahwa dalam perjalanan, Xuanwu (玄武) berada di belakang, Naga Biru-Hijau (青龍) di kiri, dan Harimau Putih (白虎) di kanan, dengan Zhaoyao (招摇) di atas.
claims.quote: 而後玄武，左青龍而右白虎，招摇在上，急繕其怒。進退有度，左右有局，各司其局。

claims.statement: Bai Ze is a Chinese legendary being knowledgeable about spirits and deities.
claims.statement_id: Bai Ze adalah makhluk gaib legenda Tiongkok yang mengetahui persoalan roh dan dewa.
claims.quote: Bai Ze (simplified Chinese: 白泽; traditional Chinese: 白澤; pinyin: Báizé) is a mythical creature from ancient Chinese legends. During the Tang Dynasty, it was introduced to Japan with its name unchanged.

claims.statement: A tale links it to pictures of spirits commissioned by the Yellow Emperor.
claims.statement_id: Kisah menghubungkannya dengan gambar roh yang dibuat atas permintaan Kaisar Kuning.
claims.quote: Entrusted by the Yellow Emperor, Bai Ze drew all the ghosts and spirits he knew into pictures and added annotations, which is the origin of the Bái Zé Tú.

claims.statement: The SanCai TuHui describes a dragon head with green hair, a horn, and flight.
claims.statement_id: SanCai TuHui menggambarkan kepala naga dengan rambut hijau, tanduk, dan kemampuan terbang.
claims.quote: In the Ming Dynasty book SanCai TuHui (三才圖會), Bai Ze’s appearance is described as having green hair on a loong head, with a horn growing on the top and the ability to fly. In the History of Yuan (元史), it is recorded as having the head of a tiger, red mane, loong’s body, and a horn. Bai Ze’s image in China combines features of both the loong and tiger.

claims.statement: The History of Yuan gives a variant with a tiger head, red mane, and dragon body.
claims.statement_id: History of Yuan memberikan varian kepala harimau, surai merah, dan tubuh naga.
claims.quote: In the Ming Dynasty book SanCai TuHui (三才圖會), Bai Ze’s appearance is described as having green hair on a loong head, with a horn growing on the top and the ability to fly. In the History of Yuan (元史), it is recorded as having the head of a tiger, red mane, loong’s body, and a horn. Bai Ze’s image in China combines features of both the loong and tiger.

claims.statement: The surviving Dunhuang manuscript concerns spirit diagrams and contains no drawing of Bai Ze itself.
claims.statement_id: Naskah Dunhuang yang tersisa membahas diagram roh dan tidak memuat gambar Bai Ze sendiri.
claims.quote: The only existing evidence related to Bái Zé Tú in China is an incomplete Dunhuang manuscript. It is said to have been copied in the 9th or 10th century and titled “Baize-jing guai—tu” ‘Bai Ze Diagrams of Spectral Prodigies’ (白澤精惟圖), now kept at the National Library of France (P2682). This Dunhuang manuscript does not contain any drawings of Bai Ze.

claims.statement: In Japan, this being is known as Hakutaku.
claims.statement_id: Di Jepang, makhluk ini dikenal sebagai Hakutaku.
claims.quote: In Japan, Bai Ze is also called Hakutaku. The oldest known depiction of Hakutaku appears in the Tiandi ruixiang zhi ‘Treatise on the Auspicious Signs of Heaven and Earth’ (天地瑞祥志), a work originated in China. This work is listed in late 9th-century Japanese bibliographies, while it is unknown in Chinese ones.

claims.statement: According to the Yunji Qiqian, the Yellow Emperor, touring east to the sea and climbing Mount Huan, obtained the divine beast Bai Ze on the coast; it could speak and understood the nature of all things. He asked about ghosts and spirits; Bai Ze named 11,520 kinds, the emperor had them drawn to show the world, and composed a text for warding off evil.
claims.statement_id: Menurut Yunji Qiqian, Kaisar Kuning dalam perjalanan keliling ke timur sampai laut, mendaki Gunung Huan, dan di pantai mendapatkan binatang gaib Bai Ze yang dapat berbicara dan memahami keadaan segala hal. Ia bertanya tentang urusan hantu dan roh; Bai Ze menyebutkan 11.520 jenis, kaisar memerintahkan agar digambar untuk ditunjukkan ke seluruh dunia, dan menyusun naskah penangkal kejahatan.
claims.quote: 帝巡狩東至海，登桓山，於海濱得白澤神獸，能言，達於萬物之情。因問天下鬼神之事，自古精氣為物，游魂為變者，凡萬一千五百二十種，白澤言之，帝令以圖寫之以示天下，帝乃作《祝邪之文》以祝之。

claims.statement: Li Shizhen (Bencao Gangmu) writes that spirit-monsters (精怪) are numerous and harm people, and that books such as the Baize Tu, Xuanzhong Ji, Baopuzi and Youyang Zazu record them in considerable detail, so that those who live among them should know them.
claims.statement_id: Li Shizhen (Bencao Gangmu) menulis bahwa makhluk-makhluk jelmaan (精怪) banyak dan merugikan manusia, dan bahwa kitab seperti Baize Tu, Xuanzhong Ji, Baopuzi, dan Youyang Zazu mencatatnya dengan cukup lengkap sehingga orang yang tinggal di dalamnya perlu mengetahuinya.
claims.quote: 精怪之屬甚伙，皆為人害。惟《白澤圖》、《玄中記》、《抱朴子》、《酉陽雜俎》諸書載之頗悉，起居者亦不可不知。

claims.statement: Li Shizhen quotes the Baize Tu that the spirit of trees is named Penghou (彭侯), looks like a black dog without a tail, and can be cooked and eaten.
claims.statement_id: Li Shizhen mengutip Baize Tu bahwa roh pohon bernama Penghou (彭侯) berbentuk seperti anjing hitam tanpa ekor dan dapat dimasak untuk dimakan.
claims.quote: 時珍曰︰按《白澤圖》云︰木之精名曰彭侯，狀如黑狗，無尾，可烹食。

claims.statement: In the folk beliefs of imperial China, Bai Ze also symbolized the ability to expel ghosts and ward off evil spirits.
claims.statement_id: Dalam kepercayaan rakyat Tiongkok kekaisaran, Bai Ze juga melambangkan kemampuan mengusir hantu dan menangkal roh jahat.
claims.quote: In the folk beliefs of imperial China, Bai Ze also symbolized the ability to expel ghosts and ward off evil spirits.

claims.statement: In the Tiandi ruixiang zhi, Hakutaku has a cow's body and a bearded human head; the "Hakutaku hi kai zu" painted by Fukuhara Gogaku has three faces, each with three eyes and a pair of horns.
claims.statement_id: Dalam Tiandi ruixiang zhi, Hakutaku bertubuh sapi dan berkepala manusia berjenggot; lukisan "Hakutaku hi kai zu" oleh Fukuhara Gogaku memperlihatkan tiga wajah, masing-masing bermata tiga dan bertanduk sepasang.
claims.quote: In Tiandi ruixiang zhi, Hakutaku has the body of a cow and a human head with a beard. The “Hakutaku hi kai zu” image painted by Fukuhara Gogaku features three faces, each with three eyes and a pair of horns.

claims.statement: During the cholera epidemic in Edo in 1858, people were instructed to place Hakutaku's image on their pillows before going to bed to protect themselves.
claims.statement_id: Pada wabah kolera di Edo tahun 1858, orang diinstruksikan menaruh gambar Hakutaku di bantal sebelum tidur untuk melindungi diri.
claims.quote: During the cholera epidemic in Edo in 1858, people were instructed to place Hakutaku’s image on their pillows before going to bed to protect themselves.

claims.statement: Manimekhala is a sea-guardian goddess in Southeast Asian Hindu-Buddhist mythology.
claims.statement_id: Manimekhala adalah dewi penjaga laut dalam mitologi Hindu-Buddhis Asia Tenggara.
claims.quote: Manimekhala (Pali: Maṇīmekhalā) is a goddess in the Hindu-Buddhist mythology. She is regarded as a guardian of the seas, namely the Indian Ocean and the South China Sea as part of the mythology of Southeast Asia. She was placed by Cātummahārājika to protect virtuous beings from shipwreck.

claims.statement: In the Mahajanaka Jataka, she rescues Prince Mahajanaka from a shipwreck.
claims.statement_id: Dalam Mahajanaka Jataka, ia menyelamatkan Pangeran Mahajanaka dari kapal karam.
claims.quote: She appears in several Buddhist stories including the Mahanipata Jataka (Mahajanaka Jataka), in which she rescues Prince Mahajanaka from a shipwreck.

claims.statement: The Pali name maṇīmekhalā denotes a jeweled girdle.
claims.statement_id: Nama Pali maṇīmekhalā berarti sabuk permata.
claims.quote: In Pali, maṇīmekhalā refers to a girdle or belt of jewels. In Southeast Asia, she is known by various indigenized appellations, including as Mani Maykhala (မဏိမေခလာ) in Burmese, as Moni Mekhala (មណីមេខលា) or Neang Mekhala (នាងមេខលា) in Khmer; as Mani Mekkhala (มณีเมขลา) in Thai.

claims.statement: Reliefs of her from the first millennium CE were found at Zothoke, Myanmar.
claims.statement_id: Reliefnya ditemukan di Zothoke, Myanmar, dan berasal dari milenium pertama Masehi.
claims.quote: Archaeological evidence of Manimekhala in the form of reliefs has been found in Zothoke, Myanmar (near Bilin), dating to the first millennium AD.

claims.statement: In Thailand and Cambodia, she is associated with lightning and the seas.
claims.statement_id: Di Thailand dan Kamboja, ia dikaitkan dengan kilat dan laut.
claims.quote: Manimekhala is seen in wat paintings across Mainland Southeast Asia depicting scenes from the Mahajanaka. In Thailand and Cambodia, she is considered a goddess of lightning and the seas.

claims.statement: The Ramasura pursuit tale explains lightning through her crystal ball and thunder through her pursuer's axe.
claims.statement_id: Kisah pengejaran Ramasura menjelaskan kilat melalui bola kristalnya dan guntur melalui kapak pengejar.
claims.quote: According to legend, the phenomena of lightning and thunder is produced from the flashing of Manimekhala's crystal ball and the sound of Ramasura's axe as he pursues her through the skies.

claims.statement: In the Mahājanaka-jātaka, a daughter of the gods named Maṇimekhalā had been appointed guardian of the sea by the four guardians of the world.
claims.statement_id: Dalam Mahājanaka-jātaka, seorang putri para dewa bernama Maṇimekhalā ditunjuk sebagai penjaga laut oleh keempat penjaga dunia.
claims.quote: Now at that time a daughter of the gods named Maṇimekhalā had been appointed guardian of the sea by the four guardians of the world.

claims.statement: The guardians of the world told her that beings possessing virtues such as reverence for their mothers do not deserve to fall into the sea, and that she should look out for such beings.
claims.statement_id: Para penjaga dunia berpesan kepadanya bahwa makhluk yang memiliki kebajikan seperti menghormati ibu tidak layak tenggelam di laut, dan ia harus mencari yang demikian.
claims.quote: They said to her, "Those beings who possess such virtues as reverence for their mothers and the like do not deserve to fall into the sea,—look out for such"

claims.statement: After helping the prince, she brought him to Mithilā and laid him on the ceremonial stone in a mango grove, then left him in the care of the goddesses of the garden and departed to her own abode.
claims.statement_id: Setelah menolong sang pangeran, ia membawanya ke Mithilā dan membaringkannya di atas batu upacara di kebun mangga, lalu menitipkannya kepada dewi-dewi taman dan kembali ke tempat tinggalnya.
claims.quote: Then she brought him to Mithilā and laid him on his right side on the ceremonial stone in a mango grove, and, leaving him in the care of the goddesses of the garden, departed to her own abode.

claims.statement: In the Master's identification of the birth, the sea-goddess at that time was Uppalavaṇṇā.
claims.statement_id: Dalam pengenalan kelahiran oleh sang Guru, dewi laut pada masa itu adalah Uppalavaṇṇā.
claims.quote: At that time the sea-goddess was Uppalavaṇṇā

claims.statement: Xiezhi is a Chinese-origin mythical creature resembling an ox or goat with one horn.
claims.statement_id: Xiezhi adalah makhluk mitologis asal Tiongkok, bertanduk tunggal dan menyerupai sapi atau kambing.
claims.quote: The xiezhi (獬豸; xièzhì < Eastern Han Chinese *gɛʔ-ḍɛʔ) is a mythical creature of Chinese origin found throughout Sinospheric legends. It resembles an ox or goat, with thick dark fur covering its body, bright eyes and a single long horn on its forehead. It has great intellect and understands human speech.

claims.statement: This creature is credited with understanding human speech and distinguishing right from wrong.
claims.statement_id: Makhluk ini dianggap memahami ujaran manusia dan membedakan benar dari salah.
claims.quote: The xiezhi (獬豸; xièzhì < Eastern Han Chinese *gɛʔ-ḍɛʔ) is a mythical creature of Chinese origin found throughout Sinospheric legends. It resembles an ox or goat, with thick dark fur covering its body, bright eyes and a single long horn on its forehead. It has great intellect and understands human speech.

claims.statement: In the Lunheng tale, Gao Yao, minister of justice for the legendary Emperor Shun, orders it to ram guilty defendants.
claims.statement_id: Dalam kisah Lunheng, Gao Yao, menteri kehakiman Kaisar Shun yang legendaris, memerintahkannya menyeruduk terdakwa yang bersalah.
claims.quote: According to legend, the xiezhi, was a single-horned sheep or goat which had power to divine the guilt or innocence of a person. Gao Yao, the minister of justice for the legendary Emperor Shun employed the beast during criminal proceedings and he would command the sheep to ram (head-butt) the accused. The beast would ram the guilty, but spare the innocent.

claims.statement: The Lunheng also mentions their images painted in public offices.
claims.statement_id: Lunheng juga menyebut lukisan makhluk dan pejabat itu pada kantor pemerintahan.
claims.quote: In the same work (Lunheng), the legend is prefaced the remark that public offices are painted with the images of the beast and the minister.

claims.statement: Chinese dynasties promoted xiezhi as a symbol of traditional law.
claims.statement_id: Dinasti Tiongkok menggunakan xiezhi sebagai lambang hukum tradisional.
claims.quote: As a symbol of traditional Chinese law, xiezhi has been promoted by the Chinese dynasties.

claims.statement: The judicial hat was named xiezhi after the mythical sheep or ox.
claims.statement_id: Topi hukum dinamai xiezhi dari makhluk berbentuk domba atau sapi itu.
claims.quote: was also referred to as the xiezhi after the mythical sheep/ox. The xiezhi hat was part of the attire of censors

claims.statement: The Shuowen passage quoted in the Taiping Yulan: the xiezhi resembles an ox with one horn; in antiquity it was ordered to butt the party in the wrong in lawsuits; asked what it eats and where it lives, the answer was that it eats jian (薦), lives by marshes in spring and summer, and among bamboo and pines in autumn and winter.
claims.statement_id: Kutipan Shuowen dalam Taiping Yulan: xiezhi menyerupai sapi dan bertanduk satu; pada zaman dahulu ia diperintah menanduk pihak yang bersalah dalam perkara; ketika ditanya makan apa dan tinggal di mana, dijawab ia makan "jian" (薦), tinggal di rawa pada musim semi dan panas, dan di antara bambu dan pinus pada musim gugur dan dingin.
claims.quote: 獬豸，似牛，一角。古者決訟，命觸不直。黃帝時有遺帝獬豸者，帝問何食何處，曰：「食薦。春夏處水澤，秋冬處竹箭松筠。」

claims.statement: The Shenyijing passage quoted in the Taiping Yulan: in the northeastern wilderness there is a beast like an ox, with one horn, blue fur and four feet like a bear; it is loyal and upright, butting the wrongful party when it sees people fighting and biting the unjust party when it hears an argument; it is named xiezhi, or "Renfa Shou" (任法獸); Zhang Hua adds that the censor's law cap of his day was called xiezhi.
claims.statement_id: Kutipan Shenyijing dalam Taiping Yulan: di tanah liar timur laut ada binatang seperti sapi, bertanduk satu, berbulu biru, berkaki empat seperti beruang; ia setia dan lurus, menanduk pihak yang salah ketika melihat orang berkelahi dan menggigit pihak yang tidak benar ketika mendengar perdebatan; namanya xiezhi atau "Renfa Shou" (任法獸); Zhang Hua menambahkan bahwa topi hukum pejabat pengawas masa itu disebut xiezhi.
claims.quote: 東北荒中有獸，如牛，一角，毛青，四足，似熊。忠直，見人斗則觸不直，聞人論則咋不正。名曰獬豸，一名任法獸。〈張華曰：今御史法冠曰獬豸。〉

claims.statement: The Lunheng passage quoted in the Taiping Yulan: the xiezhi is a one-horned sheep that by nature recognises the guilty; Gao Yao (皋繇) had it butt the guilty in trials, and revered it, kneeling to serve it.
claims.statement_id: Kutipan Lunheng dalam Taiping Yulan: xiezhi adalah kambing bertanduk satu yang secara naluri mengenali orang bersalah; Gao Yao (皋繇) memerintahkannya menanduk yang bersalah dalam pengadilan, dan menghormatinya dengan berlutut melayaninya.
claims.quote: 獬豸者，一角之羊，性識有罪。皋繇治獄，有罪者令羊觸之。皋繇敬羊，跪坐事之。

claims.statement: The Tangshu passage quoted in the Taiping Yulan: in year 21 of the era written 開玄, a one-horned divine sheep was born in Fuping county, Jingzhao, with a fleshy horn on the crown of its head and white hair; those who knew named it xiezhi.
claims.statement_id: Kutipan Tangshu dalam Taiping Yulan: pada tahun ke-21 era yang ditulis 開玄, seekor kambing suci bertanduk satu lahir di Kabupaten Fuping, Jingzhao, dengan tanduk berdaging di ubun-ubun dan bulu putih; orang yang paham menamainya xiezhi.
claims.quote: 開玄二十一年，有一角神羊產於京兆之富平縣，肉角當頂，白毛上捧。識者以獬豸名之。

claims.statement: In Japan it is known as kaichi (獬豸), sometimes called shin'yō (神羊, "divine sheep"), and is described as similar to a lion with one horn on top of its head.
claims.statement_id: Di Jepang makhluk ini dikenal sebagai kaichi (獬豸), kadang disebut shin'yō (神羊, "domba ilahi"), dan digambarkan menyerupai singa dengan satu tanduk di puncak kepala.
claims.quote: In Japan, it is known as kaichi ... The kaichi is described as similar to a lion with one horn on the top of its head.

claims.statement: According to Korean records, the haetae has a muscular, lion-like body covered with sharp scales, a bell at its neck and a horn on its forehead, and lives in the frontier areas of Manchuria.
claims.statement_id: Menurut catatan Korea, haetae bertubuh singa berotot yang tertutup sisik tajam, berlonceng di leher, dan bertanduk di dahi; ia hidup di wilayah perbatasan Manchuria.
claims.quote: According to Korean records, the haetae has a muscular leonine body covered with sharp scales, a bell in its neck and a horn on its forehead. It lives in the frontier areas of Manchuria.

claims.statement: Bixi is a Chinese mythological figure portrayed as a dragon with a turtle shell.
claims.statement_id: Bixi adalah tokoh mitologi Tiongkok berupa naga bercangkang kura-kura.
claims.quote: Bixi, or Bi Xi (Wade–Giles: Pi-hsi), is a figure from Chinese mythology. One of the nine sons of the Dragon King, he is depicted as a dragon with the shell of a turtle.

claims.statement: He is described as one of the Dragon King's nine sons.
claims.statement_id: Ia disebut salah satu dari sembilan putra Raja Naga.
claims.quote: Bixi, or Bi Xi (Wade–Giles: Pi-hsi), is a figure from Chinese mythology. One of the nine sons of the Dragon King, he is depicted as a dragon with the shell of a turtle.

claims.statement: Bixi stone sculptures form decorative supports for commemorative steles and tablets.
claims.statement_id: Patung Bixi menjadi landasan prasasti peringatan dan makam.
claims.quote: Stone sculptures of Bixi have been used in Chinese culture for centuries as a decorative plinth for commemorative steles and tablets, particularly in the funerary complexes of China's later emperors and to commemorate important events, such as an imperial visit or the anniversary of a World War II victory.

claims.statement: The tortoise-mounted stele tradition existed by the early third century, in the late Han dynasty.
claims.statement_id: Tradisi prasasti di atas kura-kura sudah ada paling lambat pada awal abad ketiga, pada akhir Dinasti Han.
claims.quote: The tradition of tortoise-mounted stelae originated no later than early 3rd century (late Han dynasty). According to the 1957 survey by Chêng Tê-k'un (鄭徳坤),  the earliest extant tortoise-borne stele is thought to be the one at the tomb of Fan Min (樊敏), in Lushan County, Ya'an, Sichuan. Victor Segalen had earlier identified the stele as a Han dynasty monument.

claims.statement: A Nanjing Museum funerary jar dated 272 depicts a miniature stele-bearing tortoise.
claims.statement_id: Guci pemakaman Museum Nanjing bertanggal 272 menampilkan miniatur kura-kura pembawa prasasti.
claims.quote: In the collection of the Nanjing Museum there is a hunping funerary jar, dating to 272 AD, with a miniature architectural composition on top, depicting, among other objects, a tortoise carrying a stele erected by the Jin dynasty governor of Changsha in honor of a local dignitary.

claims.statement: In the first year of the Ming dynasty (1368), the Hongwu Emperor adopted regulations restricting tortoise-based funerary tablets according to rank.
claims.statement_id: Pada tahun pertama Dinasti Ming (1368), Kaisar Hongwu menetapkan aturan yang membatasi tablet makam berbasis kura-kura menurut pangkat.
claims.quote: The bixi tradition flourished during the Ming and Qing dynasties. The Ming founder, the Hongwu Emperor, in the first year after the dynasty had been proclaimed (1368), adopted regulations, allowing tortoise-based funerary tablets to the higher ranks of the nobility and the mandarinate.

claims.statement: Chinese dictionaries translate the word bi 贔 or bixi 贔屭 (also written with the variant 贔屓) as "strong" and "capable to support great weight".
claims.statement_id: Kamus Tionghoa menerjemahkan kata bi 贔 atau bixi 贔屭 (dengan varian tulisan 贔屓) sebagai "kuat" dan "mampu menopang beban berat".
claims.quote: The word bi 贔 or bixi 贔屭 (also written with a variant character, 贔屓) is translated by Chinese dictionaries as "strong", "capable to support great weight".

claims.statement: According to this article, Zuo Si in his Wu Capital Rhapsody (Wu Jing Fu) associates the attribute bixi with the legendary giant turtle ao, whose head supports a sacred mountain.
claims.statement_id: Menurut artikel ini, Zuo Si dalam Wu Jing Fu mengaitkan sifat bixi dengan kura-kura raksasa legendaris ao yang kepalanya menopang gunung suci.
claims.quote: Zhang Heng's follower, Zuo Si (250–305), in his Wu Capital Rhapsody (Wu Jing Fu), explicitly associates the attribute bixi with the legendary giant turtle ao, whose head supports a sacred mountain.

claims.statement: Bixi sculptures are traditionally rubbed for good luck, which can cause conservation problems.
claims.statement_id: Patung Bixi secara tradisional digosok untuk keberuntungan, yang dapat menimbulkan masalah pelestarian.
claims.quote: Sculptures of Bixi are traditionally rubbed for good luck, which can cause conservation issues.

claims.statement: This text records two lists of the dragon's sons: in one, Baxia (霸下) likes to carry weight and serves as a stele base while Xibi (屭贔) likes literature and stands at the sides of the stele; in the Bowuzhi (Yipian), Xibi likes to bear weight and is therefore used to carry stone steles. The text notes that the two lists differ in names.
claims.statement_id: Teks ini mencatat dua daftar anak naga: menurut satu daftar, Baxia (霸下) gemar memikul beban dan menjadi alas prasasti sedangkan Xibi (屭贔) gemar sastra dan berada di sisi prasasti; menurut Bowuzhi (Yipian), Xibi gemar memikul beban sehingga dipakai membawa prasasti batu. Teks menyatakan bahwa kedua daftar itu berbeda dalam nama.
claims.quote: 又龍九子，一名霸下，好負重，故為碑座；屭贔，好文，在碑文兩旁。亦出《總龜》。《博物志•逸篇》又云：「屭贔性好負重，故用載石碑，螭虎形似龍，性好文采，故立於碑文上。」二說名字亦不同。

claims.statement: In another list of the dragon's sons, the one that likes to carry heavy loads and serves as the stele base is Baxia (霸下), while Xixi (屓屭) likes literature and stands at the sides of steles.
claims.statement_id: Dalam daftar anak naga lain, yang gemar memikul beban dan menjadi dasar prasasti adalah Baxia (霸下), sedangkan Xixi (屓屭) gemar sastra dan berada di sisi prasasti.
claims.quote: 霸下，好負重，為碑座。狴犴，好訟，為獄門。屓屭，好文，在碑兩傍。

claims.statement: According to this article, Li Dongyang and Xie Zhaozhe call the stele-carrying tortoise baxia (霸下) rather than bixi, and apply the name bixi to the "literature-loving" dragons on the sides of the stele.
claims.statement_id: Menurut artikel ini, Li Dongyang dan Xie Zhaozhe menyebut kura-kura pembawa prasasti dengan nama baxia (霸下), bukan bixi, dan memakai nama bixi untuk naga "pencinta sastra" di sisi prasasti.
claims.quote: both Li Dongyang (1441–1516), in his Huai Lu Tang Ji, and Xie Zhaozhe (謝肇淛, 1567–1624), in his Wu Za Zu (五雜俎, Five Assorted Offerings, ca. 1592), refer to the tortoise that carries the stele by the name baxia (霸下), rather than bixi; at the same time they apply the name bixi to the "literature-loving" dragons that appear on the sides of the stele

claims.statement: Another list quoted in this text says that Xibi (屭贔) looks like a tortoise, likes bearing weight, and is therefore used to carry stone steles.
claims.statement_id: Daftar lain yang dikutip dalam teks ini menyebut bahwa Xibi (屭贔) berbentuk seperti kura-kura, gemar memikul beban, sehingga dipakai untuk menopang prasasti batu.
claims.quote: 屭贔，其形似龜，性好負重，故用載石碑。螭𧉚，其形似獸，性好望，故立屋角上。

claims.statement: The author of this text recalls seeing the account in a book at about age eleven or twelve, and after examining written records concluded that the account of the dragon's nine sons is unfounded (不經).
claims.statement_id: Penulis teks ini mengingat pernah melihat kisah itu dalam sebuah buku ketika berusia sekitar sebelas atau dua belas tahun, dan setelah memeriksa catatan tertulis ia menyimpulkan kisah tentang sembilan anak naga itu tidak berdasar (不經).
claims.quote: 余憶十一、二時，曾見其說於《對類總龜》中，近因歴考傳記，乃知其說為不經。

claims.statement: The Snow Lion is a Tibetan celestial animal symbolizing snowy mountains.
claims.statement_id: Snow Lion adalah hewan surgawi Tibet yang melambangkan pegunungan bersalju.
claims.quote: The Snow Lion (sometimes spelled snowlion; Tibetan: གངས་སེང་གེ་, Wylie: gangs seng ge; Chinese: 雪獅) is a celestial animal of Tibet. It is the emblem of Tibet, representing the snowy mountain ranges and glaciers of Tibet, and may also symbolize power and strength, and fearlessness and joy, east and the earth element. It is one of the Four Dignities.

claims.statement: It is commonly portrayed as white with a turquoise mane.
claims.statement_id: Penampilannya lazim putih dengan surai pirus.
claims.quote: It ranges over the mountains, and is commonly pictured as being white with a turquoise mane.

claims.statement: Snow lions appeared on Tibetan emblems, currency, stamps and flags from 1909 until 1959; the two-lion version was introduced by the 13th Dalai Lama in 1912 based on old military banners and is still used by the Government of Tibet in Exile.
claims.statement_id: Singa salju digunakan pada lambang, uang, perangko, dan bendera Tibet dari 1909 sampai 1959; versi dengan dua singa salju diperkenalkan oleh Dalai Lama ke-13 pada 1912 berdasarkan panji militer lama, dan masih dipakai oleh Pemerintah Tibet di Pengasingan.
claims.quote: From 1909 until 1959, a single snow lion or a pair of them was used as the national emblem of Tibet on coins, postage stamps, banknotes and the national flag of Tibet. The version shown on right with two Snow Lions was introduced by the 13th Dalai Lama in 1912 based on old military banners, and is still used by the Government of Tibet in Exile.

claims.statement: Tales and proverbs place it as king of beasts in the highest mountains.
claims.statement_id: Cerita dan peribahasa menempatkannya sebagai raja hewan di gunung tertinggi.
claims.quote: Snow lion is frequently mentioned in Tibetan folk songs and proverbs. It is thought to live in the highest mountains as it is the "king of beasts" that would tower over other animals of the lower levels. Snow lions may also represent hermits and yogis who live high up in the mountains.

claims.statement: Tibetan lore describes Gesar and Milarepa as raised by snow lionesses.
claims.statement_id: Kisah Tibet menyebut Gesar dan Milarepa dibesarkan oleh singa salju betina.
claims.quote: In Tibetan lore, two Tibetan culture heroes, Gesar and Milarepa, were said to have been raised by snow lioness. The milk of the Snow Lioness (Tibetan: Gangs Sengemo) is reputed to contain special nutrients to heal the body and restore it to harmony. Some holy medicinal remedies are believed to contain the essence of Snow Lioness milk.

claims.statement: One legend says the lioness produces milk through her paws.
claims.statement_id: Sebuah legenda mengatakan singa betina menghasilkan susu melalui telapak kakinya.
claims.quote: Legend has it that the lioness produces milk from its paws, and the milk may pass into hollow balls given to the lioness to play with. This ball may be represented in Tibetan art as a three-coloured "wheel of joy" (dga' 'khyil).

claims.statement: According to the Central Tibetan Administration, the banner of the Ya-ru To regiment showed a pair of snow lions facing each other, and that of Ya-ru Ma a snow lion standing upright and springing toward the sky.
claims.statement_id: Menurut Administrasi Tibet Pusat, panji resimen Ya-ru To bergambar sepasang singa salju yang berhadapan, dan panji Ya-ru Ma bergambar seekor singa salju berdiri tegak melompat ke arah langit.
claims.quote: The banner of Ya-ru To regiment had a pair of snow lions facing each other, that of Ya-ru Ma a snow lion standing upright, springing upwards towards the sky

claims.statement: In the reign of the seventh-century king Songtsen Gampo, Tibet was one of the mightiest empires in Central Asia, and each regiment of its army had its own banner.
claims.statement_id: Pada masa Raja Songtsen Gampo di abad ke-7, Tibet adalah salah satu kekaisaran terkuat di Asia Tengah, dan tiap resimen pasukannya memiliki panji sendiri.
claims.quote: During the reign of the seventh-century king, Songtsen Gampo, Tibet was one of the mightiest empires in Central Asia. Tibet, then, had an army of 2,860,000 men. Each regiment of the army had its own banner.

claims.statement: According to the Central Tibetan Administration, the pair of snow lions on the Tibetan national flag stand proudly with manes of fearlessness, representing the country's victorious accomplishment of a unified spiritual and secular life.
claims.statement_id: Menurut Administrasi Tibet Pusat, sepasang singa salju pada bendera nasional Tibet berdiri bangga dengan surai tanpa rasa takut, melambangkan keberhasilan negeri itu menyatukan kehidupan rohani dan duniawi.
claims.quote: On the slopes of the mountain a pair of snow lions stand proudly, blazing with the manes of fearlessness, which represent the country's victorious accomplishment of a unified spiritual and secular life.

claims.statement: He Bo, or Hebo, is the Yellow River deity in Chinese mythology.
claims.statement_id: He Bo atau Hebo adalah dewa Sungai Kuning dalam mitologi Tiongkok.
claims.quote: Hebo (Chinese: 河伯; lit. 'Lord of the River'), also known as Bingyi (冰夷), is the god of the Yellow River (Huang He). The Yellow River is the main river of northern China, one of the world's major rivers and a river of great cultural importance in China. This is reflected in Chinese mythology by the tales surrounding the deity Hebo.

claims.statement: Bingyi is another name for this river deity.
claims.statement_id: Bingyi termasuk nama lain dewa sungai ini.
claims.quote: Hebo (Chinese: 河伯; lit. 'Lord of the River'), also known as Bingyi (冰夷), is the god of the Yellow River (Huang He). The Yellow River is the main river of northern China, one of the world's major rivers and a river of great cultural importance in China. This is reflected in Chinese mythology by the tales surrounding the deity Hebo.

claims.statement: Hebo can be understood as a personification of the Yellow River's character.
claims.statement_id: Hebo dapat dipahami sebagai personifikasi watak Sungai Kuning.
claims.quote: To some extent, the deity Hebo is a personification of the character of the Yellow River. However, Hebo has also had an important role in the history of religious worship in China (especially North China) and also having a more general function in terms of Chinese culture, including literature and poetry.

claims.statement: The Heavenly Questions poem contains a tale of Hou Yi attacking Hebo and taking his wife Luoshen.
claims.statement_id: Puisi Heavenly Questions memuat kisah Hou Yi menyerang Hebo dan mengambil istrinya Luoshen.
claims.quote: In the poem "Heavenly Questions" in the Chu Ci anthology, it is recorded: "The Emperor sent Hou Yi to reform the people of Xia. Why did he shoot Hebo and take his wife Luoshen?" The poem tells the story of Hòu Yì, a legendary archer who was sent by the Emperor to reform the people of Xia.

claims.statement: The he element in his name particularly refers to the Yellow River.
claims.statement_id: Unsur he pada namanya terutama mengacu pada Sungai Kuning.
claims.quote: The character, Hé (河) may be used somewhat generically to refer to rivers in general or to various particular flowing bodies of water. In the case of Hebo, it is particularly and primarily associated with the Yellow River of China.

claims.statement: Bo may function as an honorific associated with noble rank.
claims.statement_id: Bo dapat berfungsi sebagai gelar kehormatan yang berhubungan dengan pangkat bangsawan.
claims.quote: The contemporary meaning of Bó (伯) is generally considered to be that of an honorific title, of a martial or noble designation, similar to the European titles of nobility rendered in English as "count" or "earl". It also means uncle, as in one’s father’s oldest brother.

claims.statement: The "Hebo" (河伯) section of the Jiuge describes a speaker roaming the nine rivers with "you" (女) in a water chariot with a lotus canopy, drawn by two dragons with chi (螭) as side horses, then climbing Kunlun and looking out in all directions.
claims.statement_id: Bagian "Hebo" (河伯) dalam Jiuge menggambarkan pembicara yang berkelana bersama "engkau" (女) ke sembilan sungai dengan kereta air berpayung teratai yang ditarik dua naga dan chi (螭) sebagai kuda sisi, lalu mendaki Kunlun dan memandang ke segala arah.
claims.quote: 與女遊兮九河，衝風起兮橫波。 乘水車兮荷蓋，駕兩龍兮驂螭。 登崑崙兮四望，心飛揚兮浩蕩。

claims.statement: The "Hebo" section of the Jiuge mentions a fish-scale house, a dragon hall, a purple-shell gate, and a vermilion palace, and has its figure riding a white turtle in pursuit of patterned fish.
claims.statement_id: Bagian "Hebo" dalam Jiuge menyebut rumah bersisik ikan, aula naga, gerbang kerang ungu, dan istana merah, serta tokohnya menunggang kura-kura putih sambil mengejar ikan berpola.
claims.quote: 魚鱗屋兮龍堂，紫貝闕兮朱宮。 靈何為兮水中，乘白黿兮逐文魚。

claims.statement: In the Qiushui chapter of the Zhuangzi, Hebo (河伯) is delighted and thinks all the beauty of the world is in himself; he follows the current east to the North Sea, looks out and cannot see the end of the water, then turns his face and sighs toward Ruo (若).
claims.statement_id: Dalam bab Qiushui Zhuangzi, Hebo (河伯) merasa senang dan mengira keindahan dunia seluruhnya ada pada dirinya, lalu menyusuri arus ke timur hingga Laut Utara, memandang tanpa melihat ujung air, dan berbalik muka sambil menghela napas ke arah Ruo (若).
claims.quote: 不辯牛馬，於是焉，河伯欣然自喜，以（爲）天下之美，爲盡在己。順流而東行，至於北海，東面而視，不見水端，於是焉，河伯始旋其面目，望洋向若而歎

claims.statement: Nian is a beast in Chinese tales said to inhabit the sea or mountains.
claims.statement_id: Nian adalah makhluk dalam kisah Tiongkok yang tinggal di laut atau gunung.
claims.quote: A nian beast (traditional Chinese: 年獸; simplified Chinese: 年兽; Hanyu Pinyin: Nián shòu; Tongyong Pinyin: Nián shòu; Wade–Giles: Nien2 shou4; Cantonese Yale: Nìhn sau; Zhuyin Fuhao: ㄋㄧㄢˊ ㄕㄡˋ) is a beast in Chinese mythology. According to Chinese mythology, the nian lives under the sea or in the mountains. The Chinese character nian more usually means "year" or "new year".

claims.statement: The earliest written sources describing Nian as a creature date from the early 20th century.
claims.statement_id: Catatan tertulis tentang Nian sebagai makhluk baru diketahui dari awal abad kedua puluh.
claims.quote: The earliest written sources that refer to the nian as a creature date to the early 20th century.

claims.statement: The tale describes it emerging at New Year to feed on people and animals.
claims.statement_id: Kisah menyebutnya keluar pada tahun baru untuk memangsa manusia dan hewan.
claims.quote: Once every year at the beginning of Chinese New Year, the nian would come out of its hiding place to feed, mostly on people and animals. During the winter, when food was scarce, it would raid villages, eating the crops and sometimes the villagers themselves - particularly their children.

claims.statement: Nian's appearance varies, including a flat-faced lion with a dog's body.
claims.statement_id: Penampilan Nian memiliki varian, termasuk singa berwajah datar dengan tubuh anjing.
